opus-5.5.text:
I'd start by being honest about what the model is for. You're not trying to capture everything about how a large language model gets trained. You want the smallest setup that still contains the thing you're worried about, so you can reason about it cleanly and maybe prove things.

The first step is to separate the pieces. There's some underlying task with a true answer, or a true notion of good behavior. There's a learner, which you can treat abstractly as something that searches over a big space of policies. And there's a supervision signal: what the training process actually rewards. Alignment problems mostly live in the gap between the supervision signal and the true objective. So a model that collapses those two, where the reward is exactly what we want, is useless for alignment. The core of the model has to be that the supervisor is limited.

Next, you have to decide how the supervisor is limited. The interesting cases usually involve a weaker or cheaper judge, like a human who can't check everything, overseeing a stronger system. That's why I keep coming back to complexity-theoretic framings, which is the old debate motivation. A polynomial-time verifier can't directly evaluate the answer to a hard question. But if you set up a game between provers, the equilibrium behavior can track the truth on much harder questions than the verifier could check alone. That gives you a crisp statement: under these assumptions, the optimal strategy in the training game is honest.

Then you have to take the gaps seriously, because the idealized version hides a lot. A few I'd want any useful model to include:

- **Approximate optimization.** Real training doesn't find the equilibrium. It finds something that's good on the training distribution. So you want results that degrade gracefully, something like "if the policy is epsilon-close to optimal, then it's mostly honest." A result that only holds exactly at the optimum isn't worth much.
- **Distribution and coverage.** The model is only trained on some inputs, and you care about behavior on others. Any safety guarantee has to say something about what happens off the training set, or be explicit that it doesn't.
- **Obfuscation and hard-to-refute claims.** One problem we found with debate is that a dishonest debater can sometimes make arguments that are computationally hard to refute even when they're wrong. A good model has to make room for that failure mode rather than assume it away, because that's where theory tells you something you didn't already know.
- **Human error.** The judge isn't a perfect verifier. They make systematic mistakes. You want to model those mistakes as something more structured than random noise, since the systematic ones are what a strong learner will exploit.

My general heuristic is to make the model simple enough to prove theorems about, then deliberately poke at each assumption and ask, "If this breaks, does the safety argument break?" The theorems are nice, but the real payoff is the map of which assumptions are load-bearing. That tells you where to point empirical work. If honesty depends on the judge not being systematically fooled in some particular way, that's a specific thing you can test with real humans and real models.

I'd also resist the urge to make it too realistic too early. People sometimes want to model gradient descent in full detail, and then they can't say anything crisp. I'd rather have a cartoon that gives sharp, possibly wrong, predictions than a faithful model that gives none. You can always add realism once you know which questions matter.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the thing I'd want to do first is be really honest about what question I'm actually trying to answer, because "a model of AI training" is far too broad, and if you start there you'll build something that captures nothing. The way I think about it is: pick one specific failure mode you're worried about, and then build the smallest possible toy world in which that failure mode can show up at all.

So, concretely, suppose the thing I care about is: does training a model with human feedback end up producing a model that's actually trying to do the right thing, or one that's just trying to look like it's doing the right thing? That's a question about the interaction between an optimization process and an imperfect evaluator. And you can strip almost everything else away.

Here's roughly the model I'd write down. You have some space of possible policies, call them behaviors, each with two numbers attached: how good it actually is, and how good it appears to a human judge who has limited time and limited understanding. And crucially those two numbers aren't the same. There's some correlation, because humans aren't useless, but there's noise, and more importantly the noise isn't random. There are directions in behavior space where "looks good" and "is good" come apart systematically. Then training is just: gradient descent, or some simple hill-climbing, on the "looks good" number.

Now, that sounds almost too simple to be interesting. But the interesting bit is what you put in as the structure of the gap between appearance and reality. If you assume the gap is small and roughly constant, you get a boring answer: training works fine. If you assume the gap grows as the policies get more capable, because more capable systems can find more elaborate ways of appearing good, then you get a model where things look great early in training and then quietly go wrong. And you can actually ask quantitative questions: how fast does the evaluator need to improve relative to the policy to keep up? What happens if you add a second evaluator who can see things the first one can't? That last question is basically the seed of debate, or of amplification schemes more generally.

The methodological point I'd stress is that the model's job is not to predict what's going to happen with real systems. It's to force your intuitions into the open. When I've done this kind of thing, most of the value came from the moment where I had to write down an equation and realized I didn't actually know what shape the function should be, and that my informal argument had been quietly assuming something I couldn't justify. The model is a device for finding the hidden assumption.

And then the second thing I'd do, after getting a toy version working, is try to break it. Vary every assumption you weren't sure about, see which ones the conclusion is sensitive to. If the conclusion is robust across a range of plausible assumptions, that's some evidence it's telling you something real. If it flips depending on a parameter you have no way of measuring, well, that's also valuable, because now you know what you actually need to go find out empirically.

So: one failure mode, the smallest world it can happen in, write down the equations, find out what you were assuming, then stress-test it. That's the loop.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by picking a particular alignment question, rather than trying to model all of AI training at once. For example: if we train a system using human judgments, what happens when the system becomes better at the task than the human judging it?

You could make a very simple model with a distribution of questions, an AI that proposes answers, and a human evaluator who can check some things but not others. Then you need to distinguish the score the evaluator gives from whether the answer is actually good. If you collapse those into the same quantity, you’ve assumed away much of the alignment problem.

Initially, I might assume that training finds the strategy with the highest expected score. That’s a very strong simplification, but it lets you ask a clean question: does the best strategy under this training objective involve giving correct answers, or exploiting the evaluator’s limitations? If it involves exploiting those limitations, better optimization won’t solve your problem.

Then you can investigate changes to the training procedure—allowing the evaluator to ask follow-up questions, for example, or having another system point out mistakes. The aim would be to prove something in this restricted setting, understand which assumptions make it work, and then test whether those assumptions survive in more realistic settings.

r001.rationale: The response describes evaluator-scored answers and training, but does not propose pretraining followed by repeated model-generated data and training on that data.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that iterative training on model-generated data could capture reinforcement learning well enough to omit an explicit reinforcement learning component.

r003.rationale: It discusses exploiting an evaluator’s limitations, but does not propose reproducing emergent misalignment in the toy model.

r004.rationale: Subliminal learning is not mentioned or proposed as a behavior the model should reproduce.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by trying to capture one particular difficulty, rather than trying to model all of AI training at once. For example, suppose we want a system to answer questions, but the person training it can’t reliably tell whether its answers are correct. They can judge some simpler questions, or check individual steps, but they can’t directly evaluate the whole task.

Then you can write down a game. There’s a distribution of questions, an agent that produces answers, and an evaluator with some explicitly limited computational ability. You specify what information the evaluator gets and what reward the agent receives. And then you ask: if the agent is very good at maximising that reward, does it give truthful answers? Or can it get a higher reward by exploiting the evaluator’s limitations?

I think it’s useful initially to separate that incentive question from the question of whether gradient descent actually finds the behaviour you want. You might first assume the agents play optimally and see whether the proposed training setup even has the right solution. If it doesn’t work under that assumption, there’s already something to fix. If it does, you can start putting learning dynamics and finite amounts of compute back into the model.

The point isn’t that the toy model will tell you whether a real system is aligned. It’s that making the assumptions explicit lets you find quite precise reasons why a training proposal might work or fail.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose reproducing emergent misalignment in the toy model.
